title: Kwek-kwek
intro: Hard-boiled quail eggs dunked in a bright orange batter and deep-fried until the shell turns crisp. Eaten hot off a skewer with a sharp, spiced vinegar dip.

items.name: annatto powder
items.note: or a few drops of orange food coloring

steps.text: Put the quail eggs in a pot, cover with cold water and bring to a boil. Boil for 4 minutes.
Drain and cover the eggs with cold water. When cool, roll each one gently on the counter to crack the shell all over and peel.
Stir together the vinegar, cucumber, onion, garlic, chili, salt and pepper. Set aside while you fry.
For the batter, dissolve the annatto powder in the water. Whisk in the flour, cornstarch, baking powder and salt until smooth. It should coat a spoon thickly; add a spoonful of water if it is stiff.
Heat the oil in a deep pot to 175°C (350°F).
Roll the peeled eggs in the cornstarch and shake off the excess, so the batter sticks. Drop them into the batter.
Lift the eggs out one at a time with a fork or skewer, let the extra batter drip off and lower them into the oil. Fry in batches, turning, until the coating is crisp.
Drain on a rack. Serve hot on skewers with the spiced vinegar for dipping or pouring over.

tips: Peeling is easier when the eggs are a few days old. Fry no more than 8 at a time so the oil stays hot and the coating stays crisp.

title: Tokneneng
intro: Whole hard-boiled eggs in a crisp orange batter, the bigger cousin of kwek-kwek. The coating is thin and crunchy, and the egg goes well with spiced vinegar or sweet fishball sauce.

items.name: annatto powder
items.note: or a few drops of orange food coloring

steps.text: Put the eggs in a pot, cover with cold water and bring to a boil. Lower the heat and simmer for 10 minutes.
Move the eggs to a bowl of cold water. Once cool, peel them and pat dry.
Mix the vinegar, onion, garlic, chili and salt for the dip.
Dissolve the annatto powder in the water, then whisk in the flour, cornstarch, baking powder and salt to a thick, smooth batter.
Heat the oil in a deep pot to 175°C (350°F).
Roll each egg in cornstarch, then turn it in the batter until fully coated.
Fry 2 or 3 eggs at a time, turning often, until the coating is crisp and lightly blistered.
Drain on a rack and serve hot, whole or halved, with the dip.

tips: Street stalls often use duck eggs, which have a richer yolk. They work the same way; simmer them for 12 minutes.

title: Fishballs with sweet and spicy sauce
intro: Flat, springy homemade fishballs, poached and then deep-fried until golden, served the cart way: skewered and dunked in a thick sweet sauce or its chili-spiked spicy twin.

items.name: boneless white fish fillets
items.note: such as tilapia or cream dory, skinned

items.name: siling labuyo
items.note: finely chopped, for the spicy sauce

steps.text: Pat the fish dry and cut it into chunks. Pulse in a food processor with the onion, garlic, salt, sugar and pepper until it forms a smooth, sticky paste.
Add the flour, cornstarch and cold water and pulse until you have a thick, tacky dough. Cover and chill it so it is easier to shape.
Meanwhile, make the sauce. Simmer the water, brown sugar, soy sauce, onion, garlic and salt in a small pot.
Stir the cornstarch mixture, pour it in and stir until the sauce turns thick and glossy. Pour half into a second bowl and stir in the chopped chilies and chili flakes for the spicy sauce.
Bring a wide pot of water to a gentle simmer. With an oiled spoon and wet fingers, drop in heaped teaspoons of dough and flatten each into a disc about 1 cm (1/2 in) thick.
Poach in batches until the fishballs float and feel firm. Lift out with a slotted spoon and drain well.
Heat the oil in a deep pan to 175°C (350°F). Fry the poached fishballs in batches until golden and slightly puffed.
Drain, thread onto skewers and serve with both sauces for dipping or spooning over.

tips: Poached fishballs freeze well for a month; fry them straight from the freezer for 4 to 5 minutes. The sauce keeps for a week in the fridge; loosen it with a splash of hot water.

title: Kikiam
intro: Ground pork and shrimp seasoned with five-spice, rolled in bean curd sheets, steamed and then fried until the wrapper blisters. Savory, slightly sweet and best dunked in sweet sauce or vinegar.

items.name: large dried bean curd sheets (tawpe)
items.note: cut into 4 rectangles about 20 x 25 cm (8 x 10 in)

items.name: cornstarch
items.note: mixed with 1 tbsp water, for sealing

items.name: sweet chili sauce or spiced vinegar

steps.text: Mix all the filling ingredients in a bowl with your hand until sticky and evenly combined.
Fry a teaspoon of filling in a little oil and taste it. Adjust the salt or five-spice in the bowl if needed.
Wipe a bean curd sheet on both sides with a damp cloth so it softens and does not crack. Spread a quarter of the filling in a log along one long edge, about 3 cm (1 1/4 in) thick.
Roll up tightly, fold in the ends and seal the edge with the cornstarch paste. Repeat with the rest.
Steam the rolls seam side down over boiling water until firm and cooked through.
Let the rolls cool so they firm up and slice cleanly, then cut each into 4 to 5 pieces.
Heat the oil in a pan to 175°C (350°F). Fry the pieces in batches, turning, until the wrapper is golden and blistered.
Drain on a rack and serve hot on skewers with sweet chili sauce or spiced vinegar.

tips: Steamed, cooled rolls keep for 3 days in the fridge or a month in the freezer. Thaw in the fridge before slicing and frying.

title: Squidballs
intro: Bouncy fried balls of squid and white fish with little chewy bits of squid all through them. Good with a garlicky spiced vinegar or the same sweet sauce you would use for fishballs.

steps.text: Mix the vinegar, shallot, garlic, chilies, salt and sugar and set aside.
Pat the squid and fish dry. Finely chop a third of the squid by hand and set it aside. Cut the rest of the squid and the fish into chunks.
Pulse the squid and fish chunks with the egg white, garlic, onion, salt, sugar and pepper to a smooth, sticky paste.
Add the flour and cornstarch and pulse to combine, then fold in the chopped squid. Chill the mixture so it holds its shape.
With wet hands, roll the mixture into balls about 2.5 cm (1 in) across.
Drop the balls into a pot of gently simmering water and poach until they float and feel firm. Drain well.
Heat the oil in a deep pan to 175°C (350°F) and fry the squidballs in batches until golden.
Drain, skewer and serve hot with the spiced vinegar.

tips: Keep the fish and squid very cold before processing: a warm paste turns soft and the balls lose their bounce.

title: Chicken isaw
intro: Chicken intestines wound onto skewers, grilled over charcoal and glazed with a sweet soy and banana ketchup baste. Smoky, slightly chewy and best dipped in spiced vinegar.

items.name: spiced vinegar
items.note: cane vinegar with chopped onion, garlic and chili

steps.text: Rinse the intestines under running water. Slit them open lengthwise with kitchen scissors so you can see the inside, and scrape away anything left in them.
Rub the intestines well with the coarse salt and rinse. Rub them again with the vinegar and rinse until the water runs clear and they no longer smell sour.
Bring the boiling ingredients to a boil in a pot, add the intestines and simmer until tender but still a little chewy.
Drain and let the intestines cool enough to handle. Wind them tightly onto the soaked skewers, folding back and forth like an accordion.
Stir together the banana ketchup, soy sauce, brown sugar, oil and garlic for the baste.
Grill the skewers over medium-hot charcoal or on a grill pan, turning and basting often, until glazed and charred in spots.
Serve hot with spiced vinegar for dipping.

tips: Many wet markets sell chicken intestines already cleaned, which saves most of the prep. You can boil them a day ahead and keep them in the fridge until grilling.

title: Pork isaw
intro: Pork small intestines simmered until tender, then grilled on skewers with a sweet and salty baste until crisp at the edges. Rich and chewy, cut through with plenty of spiced vinegar.

items.name: water
items.note: for simmering, plus more for blanching

items.name: spiced vinegar
items.note: cane vinegar with chopped onion, garlic and chili

steps.text: Turn the intestines inside out by pushing a chopstick through them, or slit them open with scissors. Scrape off any residue under running water.
Rub well with the coarse salt, rinse, then rub with the vinegar and rinse again. Repeat until they are clean and the water runs clear.
Cover the intestines with fresh water in a pot, bring to a boil and boil for 5 minutes. Drain and discard this water, which takes most of the smell with it.
Return the intestines to the pot with the 8 cups of water, cane vinegar, garlic, bay leaves, peppercorns and salt. Simmer, covered, until tender.
Drain and cool. Cut into pieces about 10 cm (4 in) long and thread 2 or 3 onto each skewer.
Mix the soy sauce, banana ketchup, brown sugar, calamansi juice and oil for the baste.
Grill over medium-hot charcoal, turning and basting often, until browned and crisp at the edges.
Serve hot with spiced vinegar.

tips: Ask the butcher for cleaned intestines if you can. The boiled isaw keeps for 2 days in the fridge, so you can do the long part ahead and grill just before eating.

title: Crispy chicken isaw
intro: Chicken intestines boiled until tender, cut short, dredged and deep-fried until they crackle. Crunchy, salty and made for dipping in sharp vinegar with a cold drink alongside.

items.name: spiced vinegar
items.note: cane vinegar with chopped onion, garlic and chili

steps.text: Slit the intestines open lengthwise with kitchen scissors and rinse under running water. Rub with the coarse salt, rinse, then rub with the vinegar and rinse until clean.
Simmer the intestines with the water, garlic, bay leaves and salt until tender.
Drain and spread on a tray lined with paper towels. Cut into 5 cm (2 in) pieces and pat them very dry, which keeps the oil from spattering.
Mix the flour, cornstarch, garlic powder, salt and pepper in a bowl. Toss the isaw in it until well coated and shake off the excess.
Heat the oil in a deep pot to 175°C (350°F). Fry in small batches, stirring, until deep golden and crisp. Keep a lid or splatter guard nearby.
Drain on a rack and serve right away with spiced vinegar.

tips: For extra crunch, fry once, let the pieces rest 5 minutes, then fry again at 190°C (375°F) for 1 minute.

title: Adidas
intro: Chicken feet braised in soy sauce and vinegar until the skin turns soft and sticky, then grilled on skewers with a sweet glaze. You eat them slowly, nibbling the tender skin off the bones.

items.name: spiced vinegar
items.note: cane vinegar with chopped onion, garlic and chili

steps.text: Cut off the claw tips with kitchen shears. Scrub the feet and peel off any patches of tough yellow skin, then rinse well.
Put the feet in a pot with the water, soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, bay leaves, peppercorns and sugar. Bring to a boil without stirring for the first few minutes.
Cover and simmer until the skin is tender but still holds onto the bones.
Lift the feet out and let them cool so they firm up. Save 1/4 cup of the braising liquid for the baste.
Thread 2 or 3 feet onto each skewer, pushing the skewer through the thick pad. Mix the baste ingredients.
Grill over medium charcoal, turning and basting often, until glazed and charred at the edges. The sugar burns fast, so keep them moving.
Serve hot with spiced vinegar.

tips: Do not boil the feet too long or the skin slides off on the grill. Braised feet keep 2 days in the fridge.

title: Betamax
intro: Cubes of set pork blood, simmered until firm, then grilled on skewers and brushed with a sweet soy baste. Soft and savory inside with a smoky, sticky outside, eaten with spiced vinegar.

items.name: fresh set pork blood (dugo)
items.note: sold in blocks at the wet market

items.name: spiced vinegar
items.note: cane vinegar with chopped onion, garlic and chili

steps.text: Cut the blood into 3 cm (1 1/4 in) cubes with a wet knife.
Bring the water, salt, garlic and bay leaves to a boil, then lower to a gentle simmer. A hard boil makes the cubes spongy and full of holes.
Slide in the cubes and simmer gently until firm and dark brown all the way through. Cut one open to check: there should be no red or runny center.
Lift the cubes out and let them cool on a plate so they firm up before skewering.
Thread 4 cubes onto each skewer, pushing gently. Mix the soy sauce, ketchup, brown sugar and oil for the baste.
Grill over medium charcoal, turning and basting, until glazed and lightly charred.
Serve hot with spiced vinegar.

tips: Buy the blood fresh from a vendor you trust, keep it in the fridge and cook it the same day. Set chicken blood works the same way. Skip this recipe if you cannot find blood sold already set in blocks.

title: Inihaw na balunbalunan
intro: Chicken gizzards simmered in soy and garlic until tender, then grilled on skewers with a sweet barbecue baste. Firm, meaty and full of flavor, a regular at every isaw stand.

items.name: spiced vinegar
items.note: cane vinegar with chopped onion, garlic and chili

steps.text: Cut each gizzard open if it is still whole, peel away the tough yellow lining and rinse out any grit. Trim off loose fat.
Put the gizzards in a pot with the water, soy sauce, garlic, bay leaves, peppercorns and salt. Bring to a boil and skim off the foam.
Cover and simmer until a fork goes in easily.
Drain and cool slightly, then thread 4 or 5 gizzard pieces onto each skewer.
Mix the ketchup, soy sauce, brown sugar, oil and calamansi juice for the baste.
Grill over medium-hot charcoal, turning and basting, until glazed and charred in spots.
Serve hot with spiced vinegar.

tips: A pressure cooker gets the gizzards tender in about 15 minutes. The simmered gizzards keep 3 days in the fridge.

title: Inihaw na atay ng manok
intro: Chicken livers marinated in soy sauce and calamansi, then grilled on skewers until browned outside and creamy inside. Rich and savory, with a sweet glaze from the baste.

items.name: chicken livers
items.note: trimmed of sinew and green spots

items.name: bamboo skewers
items.note: soaked in water; two per skewer of livers

items.name: spiced vinegar
items.note: cane vinegar with chopped onion, garlic and chili

steps.text: Rinse the livers, pat them dry and cut any large ones in half. Toss with the soy sauce, calamansi juice, garlic, sugar and pepper.
Let the livers marinate in the fridge.
Thread the livers onto pairs of parallel skewers, about 1 cm apart, so they do not spin or slip off. Mix the leftover marinade with the ketchup, brown sugar and oil for the baste.
Grill over medium charcoal, basting, for 3 to 4 minutes a side, until browned outside and no longer pink in the center.
Serve hot with spiced vinegar.

tips: Liver turns dry and grainy if you leave it on too long, so cut one open after 6 minutes: it should be just firm and evenly brown inside.

title: Walkman
intro: Pig ears simmered until tender, sliced into strips and grilled on skewers with a sweet soy baste. Chewy, gelatinous and a little crunchy where the cartilage runs through.

items.name: water
items.note: for simmering, plus more for blanching

steps.text: Singe off any hairs over a gas flame, then scrape the ears with a knife and scrub them inside and out under running water.
Cover the ears with water, bring to a boil and boil for 5 minutes. Drain and discard the water.
Return the ears to the pot with the 8 cups of water, soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, bay leaves, peppercorns and salt. Cover and simmer until a knife slides through the thickest part easily.
Drain and let the ears cool so they firm up. Slice into strips about 2 cm (3/4 in) wide and weave them onto the skewers.
Mix the ketchup, soy sauce, brown sugar and oil for the baste.
Grill over medium-hot charcoal, turning and basting, until glazed and crisp at the edges.
Serve hot with spiced vinegar.

tips: The ears slice much more neatly when cold, so simmer them a day ahead and keep them in the fridge.

title: Proben
intro: The part of the chicken stomach just before the gizzard, coated and deep-fried until crunchy outside and pleasantly chewy inside. Served on skewers with a sour, garlicky vinegar dip.

items.name: spiced vinegar
items.note: cane vinegar with chopped onion, garlic and chili

steps.text: Slit each proben open, rinse out the inside under running water and trim off any fat.
Simmer the proben in the water with the garlic and salt until tender.
Drain and pat completely dry. Toss with the calamansi juice and pepper.
Mix the flour, cornstarch, salt and garlic powder. Dredge the proben in it, pressing so the coating sticks.
Heat the oil in a deep pot to 175°C (350°F). Fry in batches until golden and crisp.
Drain on a rack, thread onto skewers and serve hot with spiced vinegar.

tips: For a thicker, craggier crust like the street carts, dip the dredged pieces in water and dredge them a second time before frying.

title: Crispy fried chicken skin
intro: Chicken skin seasoned with calamansi and garlic, lightly floured and fried until it shatters like chicharon. Salty, rich and gone in minutes, especially with spiced vinegar on the side.

items.name: spiced vinegar
items.note: cane vinegar with chopped onion, garlic and chili

steps.text: Rinse the chicken skin, scrape off any thick lumps of fat and cut it into pieces about 5 cm (2 in) square.
Toss with the calamansi juice, salt, pepper and garlic powder and let it sit.
Mix the flour, cornstarch and salt. Dredge the skin pieces, spreading them flat so every fold is coated.
Heat the oil in a deep pot to 175°C (350°F). Fry in small batches, stirring so the pieces do not stick together, until deep golden and the bubbling slows.
Drain on a rack and serve hot with spiced vinegar.

tips: The skin releases its own fat as it fries, so strain the oil afterward. It keeps for a second round of frying.

title: Balut
intro: A fertilized duck egg boiled in its shell and eaten warm: first the savory broth inside, then the yolk and the tender chick, seasoned with salt or spiced vinegar.

items.name: balut
items.note: 16 to 18 days old, from a trusted seller

items.name: spiced vinegar
items.note: cane vinegar with chopped onion, garlic and chili

steps.text: Put the eggs in a pot and cover them with cold water by about 2 cm (1 in).
Bring to a boil, then lower the heat and keep at a steady simmer until fully cooked.
Drain and serve warm, wrapped in a towel or in a basket to keep the heat in.
To eat, tap the wider end of the egg on the table and peel off a small opening. Season with a pinch of salt or a few drops of vinegar and sip the broth.
Peel away more shell and eat the yolk and chick, seasoning as you go. Leave the hard white part if you like.

tips: Balut is best eaten the day you buy it. If you are not eating them right away, keep the uncooked eggs in the fridge and cook within a day.

title: Banana cue
intro: Whole saba bananas fried in oil with brown sugar until a thin, crackly caramel coats each one, then skewered. Soft and sweet inside, crunchy and toffee-like outside.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wok or deep pan to 170°C (340°F).
Fry the bananas, turning now and then, until lightly golden and softened.
Sprinkle the brown sugar over the oil around the bananas. It will sink, melt and float back up as caramel.
Keep turning the bananas gently so they roll through the caramel and come out evenly coated and glossy brown.
Lift them out, letting the extra drip back into the pan, and thread 2 onto each skewer. Let cool for a few minutes so the coating hardens.

tips: The caramel is extremely hot. Use long tongs, keep children away from the pan and let the bananas cool before biting. Ripe saba with a few black spots gives the sweetest result.

title: Camote cue
intro: Chunks of sweet potato fried until tender, then rolled in brown sugar caramel right in the oil and skewered. Crunchy, sticky and sweet, with a soft, fluffy center.

items.name: sweet potatoes (camote)
items.note: peeled and cut into 3 cm (1 1/4 in) chunks

steps.text: Pat the sweet potato chunks dry with a towel.
Heat the oil in a wok to 165°C (330°F). Fry the sweet potatoes, stirring now and then, until a skewer slides through easily.
Sprinkle the brown sugar into the oil. Once it melts and floats up as caramel, stir the sweet potatoes so they get coated.
Scoop them out, let the extra caramel drip off and thread 4 or 5 pieces onto each skewer.
Let cool for a few minutes until the coating hardens and turns crisp.

tips: Yellow or orange camote both work. Cut the pieces evenly so they finish cooking at the same time, and be careful with the caramel: it burns badly.

title: Turon
intro: Saba banana rolled in brown sugar, wrapped in a lumpia wrapper and fried until crisp, with a crackly caramel shell. Sweet, crunchy and best eaten warm.

steps.text: Put half the brown sugar on a plate and roll each banana piece in it.
Lay a wrapper on the counter like a diamond. Place a banana piece across the lower part, fold the bottom corner over it, fold in the sides and roll up tightly. Seal the tip with a little water.
Heat the oil in a wide pan to 175°C (350°F). Fry the turon seam side down first, turning, until golden.
Sprinkle the remaining brown sugar into the oil around the turon. Turn them as the sugar melts and floats up so they get a glassy caramel coat.
Lift onto a rack or oiled plate, not paper towels, which stick to the caramel. Cool for a few minutes before eating.

tips: Fry in batches of 4 so the sugar coats each roll before it burns. Unfried turon freeze well; fry them from frozen, a minute longer.

title: Turon with langka
intro: Banana spring rolls with strips of ripe jackfruit tucked inside for a fragrant, fruity sweetness, fried crisp and brushed with a brown sugar glaze.

items.name: ripe jackfruit (langka)
items.note: fresh or from a jar, drained and cut into strips

steps.text: Roll each banana piece in the brown sugar. Lay it on a wrapper set like a diamond and add 2 or 3 strips of jackfruit alongside.
Fold the bottom corner over the filling, fold in the sides and roll up tightly. Seal the tip with water.
Heat the oil in a pan to 175°C (350°F). Fry the turon in batches, turning, until golden and crisp. Drain on a rack.
For the glaze, simmer the brown sugar and water in a small pan, stirring, until thick and syrupy.
Brush or drizzle the warm glaze over the turon and let it set for a few minutes before serving.

tips: Jarred langka in syrup is very sweet; rinse and pat it dry, or the wrappers go soggy and the oil spatters.

title: Maruya
intro: Saba bananas sliced into fans, dipped in a soft sweet batter and fried, then rolled in sugar. Crisp at the edges, fluffy around the banana and best eaten warm.

steps.text: Whisk the flour, baking powder, sugar and salt in a bowl. Add the egg and milk and whisk to a thick, smooth batter.
Cut each banana lengthwise into 3 or 4 thin slices, stopping short of the stem end so the slices stay joined. Press gently to spread them into a fan.
Heat about 2 cm (3/4 in) of oil in a frying pan to 175°C (350°F).
Dip each fan in the batter to coat both sides and lay it in the oil. Fry until golden on both sides, turning once.
Drain on a rack, then roll in sugar while still warm.

tips: If your bananas break when you slice them, just slice them through and lay the pieces side by side on a spatula; the batter holds them together.

title: Carioca
intro: Chewy balls of glutinous rice flour and grated coconut, fried until golden and coated in thick brown sugar caramel, then skewered three or four to a stick. Crisp shell, soft and stretchy inside.

items.name: grated coconut
items.note: fresh, or desiccated soaked in 1/4 cup warm water

steps.text: Mix the glutinous rice flour and coconut, then add the water a little at a time, kneading, until you have a soft dough that does not stick to your hands.
Roll into balls about 2.5 cm (1 in) across, keeping them smooth so they do not crack in the oil.
Heat the oil in a deep pot to 165°C (330°F). Fry the balls in batches, turning, until golden and crisp. Do not crowd the pot.
Drain on a rack. In a wide pan, simmer the brown sugar and water, stirring, until thick and bubbling.
Add the fried balls and toss until coated in caramel. Thread 3 or 4 onto each skewer and let cool a little before eating.

tips: If the oil is too hot, the balls brown outside before the center cooks and can burst. Keep the heat moderate and fry with a lid or splatter guard close by.

title: Ginanggang
intro: Saba bananas grilled over charcoal until soft and smoky, then brushed with margarine and sprinkled with sugar. Simple, warm and sweet, a gentler cousin of banana cue.

steps.text: Push a skewer lengthwise through each banana.
Grill over medium charcoal, turning often, until the bananas are soft and charred in spots.
Press each banana gently with a flat spatula or the back of a plate to flatten it slightly.
Brush generously with the melted margarine and grill a minute more on each side.
Sprinkle with sugar while hot and serve.

tips: A grill pan on the stove works too. Very ripe bananas fall apart on the grill, so pick ones that are yellow with only a few spots.
